title: A tale of two high streets
gist: A weekly digest piece arguing economists lose public trust because they can't tell compelling stories, then rounds up research showing visible policy (like IRA-funded manufacturing plants) moves votes, immigration raised less-educated US workers' wages, and English high streets in deprived areas are saturated with 'health-reducing' shops like takeaways, betting and vape stores.

insights.claim: Economists are poor at telling compelling stories about slow-burning economic risks, unlike the national security field which has long used speculative fiction to convey threats.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Poor narrative framing of economic risk may explain why policy warnings on issues like AI disruption or fiscal sustainability fail to move public opinion or drive action.
insights.quote: it suggests that economists can’t tell stories

insights.claim: Economist Ben Zaranko argues the profession should borrow from speculative fiction writing to make its warnings land, citing precedents from Edwardian invasion thrillers to Annie Jacobsen's 'Nuclear War: A Scenario'.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Signals a growing push within policy circles to use narrative/scenario-based communication to raise urgency on slow-moving economic threats.
insights.locator: This excellent article by Ben Zaranko

insights.claim: Zaranko points to the essay 'Europe 2031' as an example of effective economic storytelling, depicting a continent that fumbles the AI transformation and loses control of its own future.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A scenario investors should track: mainstream economic commentary is increasingly framing European AI competitiveness as an existential, not incremental, risk.
insights.quote: Europe 2031, a gripping essay imagining a continent that fumbles the AI transformation and loses control of its own future.

insights.claim: Zaranko's tongue-in-cheek proposed econ-bestseller 'Council Tax: A Scenario' highlights that UK council tax bands have gone unrevalued for so long the joke is they'll still be unrevalued when the sun burns out.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Underscores a long-dormant UK fiscal reform (council tax revaluation) that remains politically untouched despite widespread expert agreement it's overdue.
insights.quote: Council Tax: A Scenario, in which the sun burns out before our bands get revalued.

insights.claim: A study comparing a US expert panel and a representative slice of the public on ten contested economic statements found the average gap between their positions narrowed from 0.35 to 0.25 over the decade after 2013.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Public understanding of mainstream economics has been slowly converging with expert consensus over the past decade, which could support smoother reception of technocratic policy in some areas.

insights.claim: US experts and the public are broadly aligned on issues like securing semiconductor supply chains and regulating Twitter, but remain far apart on 'greedflation' and corporate price gouging as drivers of inflation.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Greedflation remains a politically live wedge issue where technocrats and voters diverge sharply, making it a persistent source of populist pressure for corporate windfall taxes or price controls.

insights.claim: The study's authors advise economists to be louder about where they agree with the public and to communicate more clearly where they diverge, in order to rebuild trust.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A prescriptive takeaway for policy communicators: selective emphasis on areas of public-expert agreement could reduce backlash against unpopular but consensus-backed policies.
insights.locator: the authors advise them to be louder

themes.theme: Clean energy manufacturing and electoral impact

insights.claim: Early studies found voters were unmoved by the Inflation Reduction Act's clean energy spending, but this was likely a measurement failure caused by analyzing counties instead of congressional districts and using overly broad treatment effects.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Earlier conventional wisdom that IRA spending had no political payoff for Democrats may be wrong once measured at the right geographic granularity.

insights.claim: Congressional districts that received a new IRA-funded clean-energy manufacturing plant recorded 1.5 percentage points higher Democratic vote share in the 2024 US election, rising by roughly 0.4 percentage points for each additional plant.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Visible, place-based industrial investment (new factories) appears to convert into measurable electoral support, a signal for how future US industrial policy may be designed and targeted politically.
insights.quote: the districts that got a plant recorded 1.5 percentage points more Democratic share on election day 2024, rising by roughly 0.4 percentage points with each extra plant
insights.locator: Redo the exercise looking just at places

insights.claim: Bold economic policy that voters can visibly see the effects of, such as a new local manufacturing plant, can produce a significant political impact even when the broader public doesn't grasp the underlying economics.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Governments seeking electoral credit for industrial policy should prioritize visible, localized projects over diffuse spending.
insights.locator: it remains the case that bold economic policy

insights.claim: The 'lump of labour fallacy' -- the belief that there is a fixed quantity of jobs so every immigrant arrival must displace a native worker -- is challenged by a study using two decades of US data and a national rather than local modelling approach.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Reinforces the economic case against restricting immigration as a tool for protecting native wages, relevant to ongoing UK and US immigration policy debates.
insights.quote: the belief that there’s a fixed quantity of jobs, so every immigrant arrival must displace somebody

insights.claim: The composition of US immigrants has shifted so that college-educated arrivals became the largest share by 2015, while the number of immigrants without a high school degree has fallen since the 2000s.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A rising-skill immigrant mix changes the labor-market competition dynamics investors and policymakers should assume when modeling wage and sectoral effects.
insights.locator: the composition of immigrants in the US has flipped

insights.claim: Immigration between 2000 and 2023 raised the wages of less-educated US-born workers by 2.6 to 3.4 percent, during a period when their real wages otherwise stagnated.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence that immigration complemented rather than undercut low-skilled native wages, countering arguments for tighter immigration as a wage-boosting policy.
insights.quote: immigration between 2000 and 2023 raised the wages of less-educated US-born workers by 2.6 to 3.4 per cent

insights.claim: The US findings suggest that reducing immigrant labor is not an effective way to raise low pay in Britain.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Directly counters populist UK policy arguments that cutting immigration would boost wages for low-paid British workers.
insights.quote: Worth a read before anyone concludes that the way to raise low pay in Britain is to send the workers away.
insights.locator: Worth a read before anyone concludes

insights.claim: A widely repeated story claimed a Welsh electricity interconnector was relocated because Harry Potter fans objected to disturbing a fan-made 'Dobby's grave' memorial at Freshwater West beach.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Illustrates how viral infrastructure-delay myths can circulate unchallenged and shape public perception of planning and energy projects.

insights.claim: Investigator Dan Davies found no evidence for the Dobby's grave interconnector story: no mention of the site in consultation responses, planning committee minutes, or contemporary press coverage, and the cable actually comes ashore at the opposite end of the beach and secured consent quickly.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Debunks a specific narrative used to characterize UK energy infrastructure planning as slow or captured by frivolous objections, a useful corrective for anyone citing the story as evidence of planning dysfunction.
insights.quote: There was no mention of the site in the consultation responses, the planning committee minutes, or any contemporary press coverage.
insights.locator: Dan Davies went looking for the evidence

insights.claim: Government attention on high streets has intensified this week amid a crackdown on vape and betting shops and the Clacton by-election.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: High street retail composition is becoming a live UK political issue, with regulatory action on vape and betting shops likely to follow.

insights.claim: In England's most deprived fifth of local areas, 'health-reducing' high street amenities such as takeaways, off-licences, betting shops and vape shops are roughly three times as prevalent as in the least deprived fifth, based on Health Equity North data.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Quantifies a structural retail-mix gap between rich and poor English high streets that likely reinforces regional health inequality, relevant to consumer/retail sector policy and health-related regulation risk.
insights.quote: the poorest parts of the country have roughly three times the level of provision as the richest parts
insights.locator: When it comes to ‘health reducing’ amenities

insights.claim: Deprived English high streets have fewer public toilets than more prosperous areas but slightly more pharmacies.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A secondary data point showing the deprivation gap in high street amenities is not uniform across all service types.

insights.claim: Meeting the UK Government's goal of halving the gap in healthy life expectancy between the richest and poorest regions will likely require policy that reshapes the retail composition of high streets in deprived areas.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Points to a potential policy lever (high street retail regulation/planning) that investors in retail, hospitality and gambling/vape sectors should watch for regulatory tightening in deprived UK regions.
insights.locator: if the Government is to meet its goal
